events.title: Everything I Want to Do In a Show | A One Woman Show
events.summary: Hi, I'm Heather Sejnow. You may remember me from such things as that Christmas Commercial for a toy store that gets played every year near St. Claire Shores; hosting shows at the Senate or Redford Theatre as dead celebrities or film characters; or living in Chicago for a short while to do Second City, iO, and then hop back to Detroit to perform at Go Comedy and Planet Ant. I've even nabbed the title of the only female stand up impressionist in the state of Michigan ( that I know of) . I haven't been on a real theatrical performance stage in a while and I'm about to turn 40. So for my mid-life crisis I'm putting on a show of "Everything I Want to Do in a Show". It's campy, crazy, and heartfelt. Most importantly, it's a love letter to everyone I've met and all the vessels of creativity I've learned along the way. Oh! And it's interactive, NSFW, and there will be some prizes for attendees. So come join me on a wild ride filled with puppets, impressions, burlesque, song, dance, and even Shakespeare. It's definitely... "Everything". Recommended for audiences 18+

events.title: Jia Yi Gu & Kate Yeh Chiu
events.summary: Material Feast Material Feast is an interdisciplinary dialogue featuring designers and practitioners interrogating the contemporary role of materials in design. Framed as a “feast,” a term that gestures toward sensory abundance, the event invites us to consider materials as processes rather than products. Designers Brittanie Dabney, Catie Newell, Meredith Miller, Melanie McClintock, and Ana Morcillo Pallarés will each give a brief presentation of their practice, using provisional objects and material samples to probe the boundaries between art, science, design, and craft. Alongside the presentations, a material library will bring together samples drawn from automotive plastic waste streams, quagga mussels from lake systems, and waste glass, as well as perforated textiles, hydrogels, and brittle sponges made from foraged “kin” species. Organized by Material Acts Material Feast is organized by Material Acts (Kate Yeh Chiu, Jia Yi Gu and Hilary Huckins-Weidner), a research platform exploring materials as cultural technique through public events centering an experimental library. The project attends to the logistical, economic, and technological actions that transform matter into the material substrate for our lives. Initiated in 2021 as part of Getty PST ART, the project has taken the form of a major exhibition at Craft Contemporary, an editorial project with e-flux Architecture, and a publication of ideas, conversations, and material inquiries. Working through exhibitions, programming, and editorial projects, Material Acts brings together theoretical and practical engagements with materials, addressing how design and architecture are entangled with social and ecological concerns. www.materialacts.org Contributors Brittanie Dabney Brittanie Dabney is the founder and CEO of Ecosphere Organics, a Detroit-based company that converts food waste from local restaurants and suppliers into reusable materials. An environmental scientist trained at Wayne State University, she studied microplastic pollution, and her company now develops compostable packaging and plant-based leather alternatives at Newlab. She is adjunct faculty at the College for Creative Studies and served on the 2025 Detroit Month of Design curatorial committee. Catie Newell Catie Newell is Professor of Architecture at the University of Michigan's Taubman College, which she joined in 2009 as the Oberdick Fellow. She is the founding principal of Alibi Studio, established in Detroit in 2010, and her work explores materiality in relation to place through material systems, light, and darkness. She is a Lucas Fellow, a Kresge Artist Fellow, and a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome. Meredith Miller Meredith Miller is Associate Professor of Architecture and Director of the Master of Architecture program at Taubman College. She holds a BS from the University of Virginia and a Master of Architecture from Princeton. With Thom Moran, she leads Post Rock, a research initiative developing a composite building product from waste plastics, and she is a founding member of the practice T+E+A+M. Melanie McClintock Melanie McClintock is Chair of Color & Materials Design at the College for Creative Studies, with an MFA from CCS and a BFA in Fashion Design from Virginia Commonwealth University. A CMF designer, multi-media artist, curator, and educator, she explores material-driven concepts of time, worthiness, and a sense of place. She worked in the fashion industry for over two decades in the United States, Qatar, and Indonesia. Ana Morcillo Pallarés Ana Morcillo Pallarés is an architect, designer, and researcher and Associate Professor of Architecture at Taubman College, teaching architectural design, design research, and spatial politics. She holds a PhD in architecture from Taubman and is developing research on the natural thermal properties of the biomatter of the quagga mussel as an opportunity for the fabrication of alternative by-products for the architectural residential industry. She is principal of Rumor Studio, formerly Morcillo Pallarés + Rule Arquitectos.

events.summary: Hybrid Lecture: Join us in Weiser Hall in person (Rooms 170 and 182) or stream live:https://myumi.ch/Z87k9 At the same moment Monet was painting the shimmering atmosphere, Rayleigh was explaining its physics. It then turns the lens around to ask how beauty, elegance, and symmetry guide physicists in their search for the laws of nature.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

legacySeriesKeys: "don't let the sun": chamber choir & university choir|hill auditorium
events.title: "Don't Let The Sun": Chamber Choir & University Choir
events.summary: WORLD PREMIERE Composer Theodore Wiprud and librettist Richard Wesley have created an oratorio examining a widespread expression of racism in America, documented in the landmark book *Sundown Towns* by the late sociologist and historian James Loewen. Conducted by Director of University Choirs Eugene Rogers, *Don’t Let the Sun*, for chorus, vocal soloists, and orchestra, will run approximately 90 minutes (plus intermission). It tells the story of “sundown towns” where residents drove out or actively excluded specific groups from residing there (from being in a town after sunset) through ordinances, signs, and acts of violence. Sundown towns excluded Black people, and in some cases, Chinese Americans, Jewish people, Native Americans, Latinas/os and other racialized groups. Since the 19th century these towns have been prevalent throughout the U.S. and especially in the Midwest, West, and East. These policies did not completely disappear over time. The attitudes that drove them morphed into housing “covenants,” redlining, discrimination within the post-war FHA and discrimination in the granting of bank loans. The results of these decisions and policies haunt our country to this very day. *Don’t Let the Sun* will shine a light on this difficult chapter in America’s ever-expanding history, and help audiences engage productively with “hard” histories. Mr. Loewen’s *Sundown Towns: A Hidden Dimension of American Racism* is the definitive history of these phenomena. Another source is the “History and Social Justice” website launched by Dr. Loewen, which has had nearly one million visitors over the last three years, and continues to amass cases and first-hand accounts. Librettist Richard Wesley’s text is inspired by the voices of individuals impacted by sundown towns and more recent policies, examining the harm experienced by both the excluded and the excluders; and recent efforts by many sundown towns to reckon with their past and shape a better future. CONTENT ADVISORY: This program explores the difficult history of sundown towns in America, including themes of racial discrimination, antisemitism, exclusion, and historical language that some audience members may find disturbing. *"Don't Let the Sun" was commissioned with support from an Arts Initiative Project Support (AIPS) grant, an Arts Research: Incubation and Acceleration (ARIA) grant, the U-M Brehm Choral Commissioning Fund and generous support from the Department of History, the Department of American Culture, and the School of Music, Theatre & Dance.* ––– *Parking / Traffic alert for attendees:* https://smtd.umich.edu/2026-construction ABOUT THE GUEST ARTISTS THEODORE WIPRUD is a composer, an educator, and a researcher on the musical community’s work toward equity and inclusion. Many of his works address social issues, including vocal works like *American Journal* (Robert Hayden) and *A Georgia Song* (Maya Angelou); and orchestral works like his Violin Concerto *“Katrina”; Wind of Many Voices*, responding to the troubled history of South Dakota; and a second Violin Concerto *“on the brink”* exploring climate grief and climate action. RICHARD WESLEY is a playwright and screenwriter whose many plays deal with social-historical moments. He wrote the libretto for Anthony Davis’ Pulitzer Prize-winning opera *Central Park Five*. Mr. Wesley has received numerous awards including the NAACP Image Award for Best Picture (for *Uptown Saturday Night*) and the National Black Theater Festival’s August Wilson Playwright Award. He teaches at New York University.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

featuredEvents.summary: Explore the intersections of performance, visual art, gender expression, and cultural resistance in Puerto Rico through a conversation with artists Freddie Mercado Velázquez and Mickey Negrón. This event delves into themes of identity and Caribbean culture.

evidence.description: The Latina/o Studies and the Contemporary Performance in Puerto Rico Working Group, in partnership with the Department of American Culture, invites you to Tropical Precarity: Drag and Visual Arts in Puerto Rico, a special performance and panel discussion. This event features an in-depth conversation with acclaimed Puerto Rican artists Freddie Mercado Velázquez and Mickey Negrón, exploring the intersections of performance, visual art, gender expression, and cultural resistance.
